name: Functional appliance orthodontics

angle.text: Orthodontists use Herbst, Twin-block and similar appliances in growing children to bring the lower jaw forward in Class II cases, improving the profile. Trials show changes, with debate over how much is skeletal versus dental.

summary: Braces-adjacent appliances (Herbst, Twin-block, Frankel) used in growing children to shift the lower jaw forward in Class II cases; trials show changes, with debate over how much is skeletal.
note: Designed for growing patients with Class II bites; outcomes in adults or for facial appearance are not covered by the trials found.
currentQuick:
Functional appliances are orthodontic devices, fixed or removable, that hold the lower jaw forward in growing children with a Class II bite (overjet, a recessed lower jaw). The best-known are the Herbst, Twin-block and Frankel appliances.
The idea of guiding jaw growth appeals to looksmaxxing communities interested in jaw projection. Randomized trials in children found favorable changes in many treated patients, but these studies concern bite and jaw relationships in adolescents, not adult facial aesthetics.
How it works: The appliance repositions the lower jaw forward and the resulting muscle forces are intended to influence growth and the position of the teeth and jaw joint. A fixed Herbst uses a telescoping rod that lets the mouth open but holds the jaw forward when closed.
Risks and caveats: Reported drawbacks include initial discomfort and chewing difficulty, unwanted spacing, and failure to complete treatment with removable designs that depend on patient wear. Treatment is done by orthodontists.
deepLead:
Functional appliance orthodontics is a group of treatments, using devices such as the Herbst, Twin-block, Frankel (FR-2), Bionator, Bass and activator appliances, that aim to modify jaw growth and bite relationships in growing patients, most often to correct a Class II malocclusion where the lower jaw sits behind the upper.
The Herbst appliance is a fixed device with a telescoping rod that holds the lower jaw forward; Emil Herbst developed it in the early 1900s and Hans Pancherz reintroduced it in 1979. A randomized trial of 215 patients aged 11 to 14 compared Herbst with Twin-block and found a lower failure-to-complete rate for the Herbst.
Randomized trials of early (preadolescent) Class II treatment, including headgear or functional appliances, report favorable growth changes in about 75% of treated children in one study. No studies found examine these appliances for aesthetic jaw change in adults.

name: Torticollis stretching

angle.text: Stretching and physical therapy for a tight sternocleidomastoid are standard for infant torticollis and are discussed in appearance circles for head tilt and facial balance. Adult use for facial symmetry has not been studied.

summary: Stretching and physical therapy for a tight sternocleidomastoid; established for infant congenital torticollis, while its use for adult head tilt or facial symmetry is not studied in the sources.
note: Evidence is for infants with congenital muscular torticollis; adult torticollis can be neurological (cervical dystonia) and is managed medically.
currentQuick:
Torticollis, or wry neck, is an abnormal tilt or rotation of the head, most often involving the sternocleidomastoid (SCM) muscle. In infants, congenital muscular torticollis is treated first with gentle stretching, positioning and physical therapy.
In looksmaxxing talk, stretching a tight SCM is raised as a way to improve head posture and neck or face asymmetry. The evidence summarized here is for infants; Wikipedia reports that about 85 to 90 percent of congenital cases resolve with conservative care.
How it works: Stretching and positioning aim to lengthen the shortened SCM and restore neck range of motion. In infants this is paired with caregiver education such as alternating feeding sides and supervised tummy time.
Risks and caveats: Adult or later-onset torticollis can have neurological or structural causes, including cervical dystonia and atlanto-axial rotatory fixation, which are medically managed, for example with botulinum toxin. Sources recommend evaluation to exclude underlying causes.
deepLead:
Torticollis, commonly called wry neck, is a condition in which neck muscles, most often the sternocleidomastoid, produce an abnormal tilt, turn or flexion of the head. It may be congenital, acquired, or spasmodic (cervical dystonia).
Stretching, positioning and physical therapy are the usual first-line approach for congenital muscular torticollis in infants. Wikipedia reports that 85 to 90 percent of congenital cases resolve with conservative care and that stretching fails in about 5 to 10 percent, who then may need surgery.
Orthopedic literature also notes that long-standing torticollis in young patients can come with flattening on one side of the face. No studies found examined stretching for facial appearance in otherwise healthy adults.

name: Cranial remolding helmet

angle.text: Parents of infants with positional plagiocephaly use custom helmets to round out a flattened skull and even the head shape. Studies exist, though high-quality evidence for benefit beyond natural improvement is described as lacking.

summary: A custom infant helmet used for skull flattening (plagiocephaly); studies exist but high-quality evidence on benefit beyond natural improvement is described as lacking.
note: Made for infants roughly 3 to 18 months old; whether it adds benefit over repositioning and natural improvement is debated in the literature.
currentQuick:
A cranial remolding helmet is a custom-fitted orthosis worn by infants with positional plagiocephaly, a flattened or asymmetric head shape, usually after repositioning has not helped. It is generally used between about 3 and 18 months of age.
The topic is relevant to appearance culture because head shape and facial symmetry are discussed there. Studies compare helmet and no-helmet groups, and Wikipedia describes high-quality evidence as lacking and use as controversial.
How it works: The helmet is shaped to leave room where the skull is flat and contact where it is prominent, so that rapid infant skull growth fills the space and reduces asymmetry.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia associates plagiocephaly with motor and language delays but states that this does not show plagiocephaly causes them. Insurers use measures like cephalic index to authorize helmets, and norms for that index have been questioned.
deepLead:
A cranial remolding helmet, also called a cranial orthosis, is a custom helmet worn by infants to treat positional (deformational) plagiocephaly, in which the skull is flattened on one side or at the back. It is typically used between about 3 and 18 months of age after conservative care such as repositioning has not corrected the shape.
Positional plagiocephaly became more common after back-sleeping guidance for preventing sudden infant death syndrome, and mild to moderate cases diagnosed before 4 months may respond to repositioning, according to Wikipedia.
Whether helmets improve outcomes beyond natural improvement is debated. Wikipedia says high-quality evidence is lacking and that helmet use for positional cases is controversial. A prospective non-randomized study of 128 infants compared helmet and no-helmet treatment.

name: Scoliosis / pelvic tilt correction

angle.text: Forum users link spinal curvature and pelvic tilt to uneven shoulders, eye line and height, and manage them for a more balanced appearance. Clinical care for scoliosis exists, while cosmetic payoffs are barely studied.

summary: Efforts to manage spinal curvature and pelvic alignment that some forum users link to shoulder, eye-line and height asymmetry; clinical care exists, but cosmetic payoffs are barely studied.
note: Scoliosis is a medical diagnosis; bracing, exercise and surgery decisions are made with clinicians, and surgery carries operative risks.
currentQuick:
Scoliosis is a sideways curvature of the spine, and pelvic tilt describes how the pelvis is angled in the sagittal plane. In looksmaxxing circles they come up as a postural foundation: people ask whether a mild curve explains uneven shoulders, a tilted eye line, or lost height, and whether correcting it would help.
Medical literature covers diagnosis, bracing, exercise and fusion surgery in detail, but it focuses on curve progression, pain and function rather than on facial balance or attractiveness. Claims that spinal correction changes facial symmetry have not been tested in published studies.
How it works: Clinically, mild curves are usually observed, growing adolescents with moderate curves may be braced, scoliosis-specific physiotherapy exercises are used in some countries, and fusion surgery is considered for large curves. Pelvic tilt is measured in adult spinal deformity research as a key parameter of sagittal balance. Forum users mainly discuss posture awareness, exercise, and occasionally surgery for height.
Risks and caveats: Surgery is a major operation with the usual risks of spinal fusion, and bracing is worn for many hours a day for years. Self-diagnosing from photos is unreliable because a diagnosis rests on examination and radiographs. Researchers have not established that correcting a small curve alters facial appearance.
deepLead:
Scoliosis is a three-dimensional curvature of the spine, usually defined as a Cobb angle above 10 degrees on a radiograph . Pelvic tilt is the forward or backward angulation of the pelvis, and in the spinal deformity literature it is treated as one of the key radiographic parameters alongside truncal inclination and sagittal balance . In looksmaxxing communities the two are discussed together as the postural base on which shoulders, neck, head position and apparent facial balance sit.
Clinical practice divides care by curve size and skeletal maturity: observation for small curves, bracing for some growing adolescents, scoliosis-specific exercise in some health systems, and spinal fusion for larger curves . A randomised trial in the New England Journal of Medicine found that bracing lowered the rate of curve progression to surgical thresholds in adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis .
No published study has tested whether correcting scoliosis or pelvic tilt changes facial symmetry or rated attractiveness. Forum discussion centres on visible shoulder or trapezius asymmetry, a tilted eye line, and whether surgery could add height; clinicians and researchers frame the condition around progression, pain, and function instead.

name: Alexander technique

angle.text: Users take Alexander technique lessons to improve posture and movement, aiming for a more upright, balanced look. Trials support it for back and neck pain, while appearance outcomes have not been studied.

summary: A century-old posture and movement re-education method with trial support for back and neck pain, but no studies on looks.
note: Evidence concerns pain and function; no published trial has examined appearance, and safety reporting in trials is sparse.
currentQuick:
The Alexander technique is a method of teaching people to notice and change habitual movement and posture patterns, typically through private lessons with a trained teacher. It was developed by the actor Frederick Matthias Alexander from the 1890s.
In appearance communities it is mentioned as a way to re-educate posture. Published trials have studied it for chronic back and neck pain and Parkinson's disease, not for appearance or facial balance.
How it works: Teachers use verbal cues and light hands-on guidance during everyday activities such as sitting, standing and walking, aiming to reduce unnecessary muscle tension and change habitual patterns. Researchers have described it as an educational approach rather than a treatment.
Risks and caveats: Few trials report safety data. Some health bodies say advocates' claims go beyond the evidence, and at least one insurer classes it as experimental. Teaching is not statutorily regulated in the UK.
deepLead:
The Alexander technique is a method of movement and posture re-education named after Frederick Matthias Alexander (1869-1955), an actor who began developing it in the 1890s to deal with voice loss during performance . It is taught in individual lessons, usually 30 to 60 minutes, using verbal cues and gentle touch during activities such as sitting, standing and walking .
Randomised trials have tested it mainly for chronic or recurrent low back pain, chronic neck pain and Parkinson's disease . The largest, the ATEAM trial in England, found that lessons reduced back-pain-related disability compared with usual care .
In looksmaxxing contexts it is listed as a way to re-educate posture. No published study has tested whether the technique changes physical appearance, facial balance or attractiveness.

name: Forward head posture exercises

angle.text: Users do chin tucks and neck-strengthening routines to pull the head back over the shoulders for a cleaner profile. The exercises are studied for neck pain, and the community debates whether they help or hurt the look of a recessed chin.

summary: Neck-strengthening and chin-tuck style routines for forward head posture; studied for neck pain, with community debate over whether they help or hurt the profile.
note: Studies link forward head posture and neck pain, but the association is not uniform and cosmetic effects are unstudied.
currentQuick:
Forward head posture (FHP, also called nerd neck or tech neck) is when the head sits ahead of the shoulders. Exercise routines for it usually aim to strengthen the deep neck flexors and upper back and stretch tight muscles at the neck and chest.
In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed both as a way to improve profile and posture and as something that might make a recessed chin look worse once the head is pulled back. Research focuses on neck pain and headache, not looks.
How it works: FHP is quantified by the craniovertebral angle. Exercise programmes target the deep cervical flexors and scapular muscles, and a trial found neck exercises improved the ability of people with chronic neck pain to hold an upright posture during a task.
Risks and caveats: Exercise itself is generally low risk, but the sources reviewed do not establish that exercise permanently changes head position or appearance. Evidence linking FHP to pain is mixed, with a meta-analysis finding an association in adults but not adolescents.
deepLead:
Forward head posture (FHP) is a posture in which the head sits forward of the shoulders, often accompanied by rounded shoulders and increased upper-back curvature. It is commonly called text neck, tech neck or nerd neck, and is measured clinically with the craniovertebral angle . Exercises for it typically aim to strengthen the deep neck flexors and shoulder-blade retractors and to stretch tight neck and chest muscles .
Research has examined the association of FHP with neck pain and headache and tested exercise regimens in people with neck pain . A systematic review and meta-analysis found a relationship between FHP and neck pain in adults .
In looksmaxxing forums, FHP is discussed as affecting side-profile and overall posture, and some users argue that correcting it can make a recessed chin look weaker. No published study has examined these appearance claims.

name: Phone neck habit change

chain: More balanced neck and upper body
angle.text: Users change how they hold and view their phone to reduce text neck, hoping for better neck and upper-body balance. Research links the posture to neck pain, while any effect on appearance or asymmetry is untested.

summary: Changing how you hold and look at your phone to reduce 'text neck'; research links the posture to neck pain, but nothing tests facial or neck asymmetry.
note: Text neck studies are mostly cross-sectional surveys; causation and appearance effects are not established.
currentQuick:
Text neck is the term for the head-down, flexed-neck posture adopted while using phones and tablets. Phone neck habit change refers to altering that behaviour, for example how long and in what posture devices are used, in the hope of reducing neck strain and, in looksmaxxing framing, neck asymmetry.
Published work on text neck concerns neck pain and posture, mostly in surveys and biomechanical models. None has measured effects on neck or facial asymmetry.
How it works: Biomechanical modelling shows neck flexion loads the cervical spine joints. Observational studies associate text neck posture and heavy phone use with neck pain in adolescents and young adults, though the link is not uniform.
Risks and caveats: Behaviour change itself carries little risk. The evidence base is mainly cross-sectional, so cause and effect, and whether altering habits changes appearance, are unestablished.
deepLead:
Text neck is a popular name for the flexed head-and-neck posture used with phones and computers, and a cluster of symptoms attributed to it, mostly neck pain . Phone neck habit change describes changing how and how long people use devices to lessen that posture. In looksmaxxing discussion the aim is often stated as reducing neck or upper-body asymmetry.
Researchers have studied text neck in children, adolescents, university students and adults, generally finding associations between text-neck posture or device use and neck pain, although authors caution that the evidence is largely observational . Biomechanical modelling of neck flexion has quantified joint loading across the cervical spine .
No study found has examined whether phone-use habits cause or change facial or neck asymmetry.

name: Beard shaping to hide asymmetry

angle.text: Users trim and outline facial hair so differences between the two sides of the lower face are less noticeable, alongside haircuts and glasses. The change in how the jaw reads is visible immediately, and it is a styling approach rather than a studied one.

summary: Using beard length and outline to camouflage uneven jaw or face; a styling idea with no studies behind it.
note: No published research tests facial hair as asymmetry camouflage.
currentQuick:
Beard shaping to hide asymmetry means trimming or sculpting facial hair so that uneven jawlines, chins or cheeks look more balanced. It is a grooming approach rather than a medical or surgical one.
No studies were found that test whether facial hair changes how asymmetry is perceived. Research on facial asymmetry itself describes how greater symmetry is rated as more attractive.
How it works: The idea is that the outline and density of a beard can visually extend or soften parts of the lower face. This is a practitioner explanation; it has not been tested.
Risks and caveats: Risks are minimal, mainly grooming effects such as skin irritation. Results depend on how much facial hair a person can grow.
deepLead:
Beard shaping to hide asymmetry is the practice of trimming or outlining facial hair so that differences between the two sides of the lower face, such as an uneven jaw or chin, are less noticeable. It belongs to style-based approaches in looksmaxxing alongside haircuts and glasses.
Facial asymmetry itself is a studied topic. Wikipedia reports that greater facial symmetry raises attractiveness ratings, particularly for female faces, and that very slight directional asymmetry is typical in the population . The same source does not discuss camouflage by hair or beard.
No studies found examining whether beard shaping alters perceived asymmetry or attractiveness.

name: Asymmetric hair part

chain: Hair falls to offset uneven sides
angle.text: Users part hair off-centre so the hair visually balances differences between the two sides of the face. The change is visible as soon as the hair is styled, and it is a styling idea rather than a studied one.

summary: Parting hair off-centre to rebalance a face with uneven sides; a styling idea with no studies behind it.
note: No published research tests hairstyle as asymmetry camouflage.
currentQuick:
An asymmetric hair part places the parting off-centre, and in looksmaxxing discussion it is proposed as a way to balance a face whose two sides differ.
No studies were found testing whether hair parting changes perceived asymmetry. Research on facial symmetry covers attractiveness ratings but not hairstyle camouflage.
How it works: The idea is that where hair falls can shift visual weight toward one side of the face. This is a practitioner explanation and has not been tested.
Risks and caveats: Risks are minimal; it is a reversible styling choice.
deepLead:
An asymmetric hair part, in looksmaxxing usage, is an off-centre parting chosen so that hair falls in a way that visually balances differences between the two sides of the face.
Facial asymmetry is a studied subject: Wikipedia reports that greater symmetry raises attractiveness ratings and that small directional asymmetry is normal in the population . It does not discuss hairstyle as camouflage.
No studies found examining the effect of hair parting on perceived asymmetry or attractiveness.

name: Brow microblading for symmetry

chain: Brow shape measured on both sides
angle.text: A technician measures both brows and tattoos hair-like strokes to even out their shape, height and fullness, with the result visible once healed. It is a semi-permanent cosmetic technique that fades and needs touch-ups.

summary: A hand-applied semi-permanent brow tattoo used to even out uneven eyebrows; it fades and needs touch-ups, and no trials test it for symmetry.
note: Largely unregulated in the US; risks include pigment migration, infection and granulomas.
currentQuick:
Microblading uses a handheld tool with fine needles to place pigment in hair-like strokes in the upper skin layer of the brows. For symmetry, the technician measures both brows and designs a balanced shape.
It is a cosmetic procedure and not a medical treatment. No clinical trial was found that tests it specifically for correcting brow asymmetry.
How it works: Pigment, usually iron-oxide based, is deposited into the upper dermis. Because it sits shallowly it fades faster than machine tattoos, lasting up to about two years with touch-ups.
Risks and caveats: Reported problems include pigment migration, colour change, hyperpigmentation, and less commonly infection, pigment reactions and granulomas. In the US it is not federally regulated and there is no standard for ink testing.
deepLead:
Brow microblading for symmetry is the use of microblading, a semi-permanent eyebrow tattoo technique, to even out differences in shape, height or fullness between a person's two eyebrows. A handheld tool with tiny needles deposits pigment into the upper dermis in hair-like strokes, and the technician plans the brow shape by measuring both sides and agreeing the design with the client.
In looksmaxxing and wider beauty culture the procedure is grouped with minor cosmetic fixes for facial asymmetry, since uneven brows are a common and visible asymmetry. Eyebrow height asymmetry is also documented in clinical settings, for example in patients with drooping upper eyelids, where researchers have studied how the brows sit before and after eyelid surgery.
Because the pigment sits in the upper dermis, microblading fades faster than machine-applied tattoos, and touch-ups are typically recommended. Reported risks include pigment migration, colour change and, less commonly, infection or granulomas. No published clinical trial was found that specifically tests microblading as a way to correct brow asymmetry.

name: Kinesiology / face taping

chain: Tape lifts or holds facial tissue
angle.text: Appearance-focused users apply elastic sports tape to the face in the hope of retraining facial muscles, holding tissue lifted and reducing puffiness for a more symmetrical look. The tape is studied for musculoskeletal use; facial use for appearance is untested.

summary: Elastic sports tape applied to the face to 'retrain' muscles; the tape's general evidence is weak and facial use is untested.
note: No studies of cosmetic facial use found; adhesive effects on facial skin not documented in the sources reviewed.
currentQuick:
Face taping borrows elastic kinesiology tape from sports medicine and applies it to the face, with the claimed aim of retraining muscles or holding tissue.
Reviews of the tape for musculoskeletal pain and strength report small or inconsistent effects, and no study of cosmetic facial use was found.
How it works: Manufacturers say the tape supports tissue, aids lymph drainage and improves proprioception. Critics and some researchers say these mechanisms are unsupported and benefits may reflect placebo.
Risks and caveats: Safety for facial use is not documented in the sources reviewed. Adhesive tape in general can irritate skin.
deepLead:
Kinesiology or face taping is the application of elastic therapeutic tape, of the kind developed for sports and musculoskeletal use, to the face. In appearance-focused communities it is described as a way to retrain facial muscles, lift or hold tissue, or reduce puffiness.
Elastic kinesiology tape was developed in the 1970s by Kenzo Kase, a Japanese-American chiropractor, and is sold under the Kinesio brand among others. Manufacturers have claimed benefits for muscle support, lymphatic drainage, pain signalling and proprioception, and published reviews of the tape in musculoskeletal conditions have reported small or inconsistent effects, with some researchers attributing reported benefits to placebo.
No published study was found that tests kinesiology tape for cosmetic facial purposes. A registered trial compares a physiotherapy technique with kinesiology taping in patients with Bell's palsy, a medical condition.

name: Facial nerve rehab / neurectomy

chain: More balanced face at rest and in motion
angle.text: This is the medical route to a more symmetrical face when facial nerve paralysis has caused droop or uneven movement, using therapy, nerve repair, grafting or muscle transfers. It is an established clinical field for paralysis; use on normal faces for cosmetic symmetry is not a studied application.

summary: Medical and surgical care for asymmetry caused by facial nerve paralysis; an established clinical field, not a cosmetic add-on for normal faces.
note: Evidence summarised here concerns paralysis patients; neurectomy outcomes were not covered by the sources reviewed.
currentQuick:
Facial nerve paralysis, most often from Bell's palsy, leaves one side of the face weak and can cause visible asymmetry. Treatment ranges from corticosteroids and rehabilitation to nerve and muscle surgery.
About 71% of Bell's palsy patients are reported to recover fully, and several rehabilitation trials are registered.
How it works: Drugs reduce nerve inflammation, rehabilitation techniques aim to improve movement, and surgery repairs, reroutes or replaces nerve or muscle function. Neurectomy means cutting selected nerve branches.
Risks and caveats: Surgical options carry the usual operative risks. Outcomes of neurectomy were not described in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Facial nerve rehabilitation and neurectomy refer to medical and surgical approaches for facial asymmetry caused by facial nerve paralysis. Rehabilitation involves therapy and exercise techniques, and surgical options include nerve repair, grafting, nerve transfers and muscle transfers. Neurectomy means cutting or removing part of a nerve.
Facial paralysis has many causes. Bell's palsy is the most common cause of acute onset, and others include infections such as Lyme disease and Ramsay Hunt syndrome, trauma, tumours, stroke and congenital conditions. About 71% of Bell's palsy patients are reported to recover fully.
In looksmaxxing discussion the topic appears as a treatment for paralysis-induced asymmetry rather than as an enhancement for people with typical faces. The sources reviewed contain no looksmaxxing-community material on it.

name: Tongue tie release

chain: Claimed shifts in face and smile
angle.text: Some forum posters discuss releasing a tight lingual frenulum in the belief that better tongue posture improves facial symmetry and smile or tooth alignment. The procedure has feeding evidence in infants; the appearance claims are untested.

summary: Frenotomy releases the tissue under the tongue; it has feeding evidence in infants, but claims about facial symmetry are untested.
note: Evidence concerns feeding and speech; no study tests it for facial appearance.
currentQuick:
Tongue-tie release cuts the frenulum under the tongue to improve tongue mobility. It is mostly used for infant breastfeeding problems, and sometimes for speech or mobility in older patients.
Online, some people link it to palate shape, jaw development and facial symmetry. These links are described as hypothesised, and no study was found testing release for appearance.
How it works: A short incision or removal of the frenulum, using scissors, a scalpel or a laser, frees the tongue. Proponents of the symmetry idea say better tongue posture could influence the palate and jaw; this is described as speculative.
Risks and caveats: The procedure is typically quick with little reported pain. Experts debate overdiagnosis of minor restrictions, and reviews describe long-term benefits for feeding duration and speech as inconclusive.
deepLead:
Tongue-tie release, also called frenotomy or frenectomy, is a minor surgical procedure that cuts or removes the lingual frenulum, the fold of tissue anchoring the tongue to the floor of the mouth, in people with ankyloglossia (tongue-tie). It can be done with scissors, a scalpel or a laser, and a related procedure, frenuloplasty, adds suturing for more complex cases.
The procedure is mainly used for infant feeding difficulties and, in some children and adults, for speech or mobility concerns. In looksmaxxing and related online discussion it is also raised as something that might influence tongue posture, palate shape, jaw development and facial symmetry. Wikipedia describes such links as possible and hypothesised and not established outcomes.
Studies of frenotomy for breastfeeding report improvement in short-term outcomes, while systematic reviews describe the evidence as of moderate quality, with inconclusive long-term effects on breastfeeding duration or speech. No study found tests release as a way to change facial symmetry or appearance.

name: Camera angle / eye dominance selection

angle.text: Users pick which side of the face and which angle to show, sometimes guided by eye dominance, so photos present the more flattering side. The change in how a photo looks is immediate. Faces are measurably asymmetric; a link between eye dominance and the best angle is not documented.

summary: Picking a 'better side' for photos; faces are measurably asymmetric, but no source links eye dominance to a flattering angle.
note: Research covers general facial asymmetry; eye dominance as a selection rule is untested.
currentQuick:
Many people photograph from a preferred side of the face, and some tie that choice to eye dominance.
Faces are known to be slightly asymmetric on average, but the sources reviewed do not say either side is preferred, and none links eye dominance to a flattering angle.
How it works: People pick the side or angle they judge as more symmetric or flattering. Eye dominance is the preference for one eye's visual input, about 70% right-dominant.
Risks and caveats: No physical risks. The practice is untested for effect on perceived attractiveness.
deepLead:
Camera angle and eye dominance selection is the practice of choosing which side of the face, and which angle, to present to a camera, sometimes with reference to a person's dominant eye. The idea is that most faces look better from one side than the other.
Research on facial symmetry reports that faces are not perfectly symmetric: on average the eyes, nose and mouth sit slightly to the left relative to the ears, so the right side of the face appears larger. Symmetry increases attractiveness ratings, more so for female faces. Wikipedia's facial symmetry article does not state that either side is preferred.
Ocular dominance is the tendency to prefer visual input from one eye; about 70% of people are right-eye dominant and 29% left-eye dominant, and it is mainly studied for aiming tasks. No source reviewed links eye dominance to choosing a flattering camera side.

name: Dental midline correction

angle.text: People pursue midline correction through orthodontics so the line between the central incisors sits in line with the middle of the face, aiming for a more symmetrical smile. The midline concept is clearly defined; reviewed sources give no evidence on its effect on perceived appearance.

summary: Aligning the centre line of the teeth; the concept is defined, but sources reviewed give no evidence on its appearance effect.
note: Little published material found; treatment details were not covered by the sources reviewed.
currentQuick:
The dental midline is the line between the upper or lower central incisors. If the upper and lower midlines do not match, it is called a deviation.
Correction usually refers to orthodontic alignment, but the sources reviewed do not describe methods or outcomes.
How it works: Orthodontic tooth movement shifts the arches so the midlines coincide. The sources reviewed give no details.
Risks and caveats: Not covered by the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Dental midline correction is the adjustment of teeth, usually through orthodontic treatment, so that the midline between the upper or lower central incisors lines up with the midline of the face or the opposing arch. The dental midline is defined as the midsagittal line of the upper and lower dental arches when the teeth are in maximum intercuspation and have ideal size, shape and position.
Each arch has its own midline, marking the contact between the central incisors. When the lower teeth shift sideways relative to the upper, the midline is considered deviated; Wikipedia's example is a lower shift of about 2 mm.
In looksmaxxing discussions, midline alignment is treated as one component of smile and facial symmetry. The sources reviewed contain no clinical studies or community material on correction methods or on how midline deviation affects perceived attractiveness.

name: Lighting / smiling side meta

chain: Light it well, even out the smile
angle.text: Looksmaxxers use side choice, lighting direction and a deliberately even smile to make the face look more symmetrical and attractive on camera and in person. The visual change is immediate in the resulting photo. It is a popular photo tactic without direct research behind it.

summary: Picking your good side, lighting it well and evening out your smile; popular as a photo tactic, with no direct research behind it.
note: Smile-symmetry research exists in dentistry, but none tests this practice.
currentQuick:
This meta covers choosing which side of the face to show, using lighting that flatters it, and practising an even smile.
It is discussed as a way to look more symmetrical in photos. Published research looks at smile symmetry in clinical settings but has not tested these tactics.
How it works: Practitioners aim to change how light and shadow fall on the face and to equalise how far each mouth corner lifts. Whether training changes smile symmetry has not been studied.
Risks and caveats: No documented harms are reported for the practice itself. Facial paralysis surgery, a separate topic, carries procedure-specific risks.
deepLead:
The lighting and smiling side meta is a set of photo-and-presentation tactics in looksmaxxing circles concerned with which side of the face is shown to a camera, how the light falls on it, and how evenly a person smiles. The stated aim is to make a face look more symmetrical or more attractive in photographs and in person by working around uneven smiles and lopsided features.
The sources available for this entry are thin. No published study has tested the practice as described by its followers, namely choosing a flattering side, adjusting lighting, or training the smile for evenness. Related clinical literature exists on smile symmetry in general dental populations  and on surgical rehabilitation of smiles in people with facial paralysis , but these concern different questions.

name: Neck training (flexion/extension)

chain: More masculine neck, jaw and frame
angle.text: Users train the neck forward and back with towels, hands, plates or machines to build a thicker neck that they say complements the jaw, posture and physique. Neck training is well studied for pain and sport performance; its effect on appearance has not been studied.

summary: Forward/back neck exercises for a thicker neck; well studied for pain and sport, not for looks.
note: Research covers pain and sport injury, not appearance.
currentQuick:
Neck training means working the neck forward and backward against resistance. Forum users promote it for a thicker neck and better posture.
Trials exist in neck pain and sport, but none test it for appearance.
How it works: Resistance exercise loads the neck flexor and extensor muscles; trials in pain and sport populations measure strength, pain and range of motion.
Risks and caveats: No harms were documented in the sources used; forum members raise questions about soreness, asymmetry and sleep apnea without published backing.
deepLead:
Neck training in the flexion and extension sense means exercising the neck forward and backward against resistance, often with a towel, hands, plate or machine. In looksmaxxing forums it is promoted as a way to build a thicker, stronger neck that proponents say complements the jaw, physique and posture.
Published research on neck training mostly addresses chronic neck pain and injury-reduction in sport, not appearance. Randomized trials in women with chronic neck pain compared high-intensity strength and endurance training , a pilot trial tested a tailored six-week program in under-19 rugby players , and a systematic review and Delphi study addressed neck training aimed at reducing head acceleration events in sport . No study found examined neck training for cosmetic purposes.

name: Neck bridges / wrestler bridges

angle.text: Looksmaxxers borrow the wrestler's bridge from combat sports to thicken the neck for a stronger, more masculine look. The exercise is documented in wrestling, judo and MMA and is mainly described for back and glute strength; its use for neck appearance has no research.

summary: A wrestling-style arch on the head and feet used to thicken the neck; no appearance research exists.
note: No data on injury risk for this use; the source material is thin.
currentQuick:
A neck bridge is an arch where the head or neck helps support the body, drawn from wrestling and grappling sports.
It is mentioned as a way to thicken the neck. No studies have tested it for that purpose.
How it works: The position loads the neck and back muscles with bodyweight. General bridge references focus on back and glute strength.
Risks and caveats: No injury data for cosmetic neck bridging were found. Any risks are not documented in the available sources.
deepLead:
A neck bridge, or wrestler's bridge, is a bodyweight position in which a person arches the back with weight supported on the feet and the head or neck, used in wrestling and combat sports and discussed in looksmaxxing circles as a way to thicken the neck. A general reference on the bridge exercise describes it as used in sporting and self-defense settings such as wrestling, judo and mixed martial arts, and as intended mainly for lower back and gluteal strength .
No studies of neck bridges for cosmetic neck thickness were found. Searches of the medical literature return mostly unrelated material, such as 'neck-bridge' devices used in aneurysm surgery, which are unconnected to the exercise.

name: Neck curls with plate

chain: Front and side neck muscles grow
angle.text: Forum users perform loaded neck curls with a plate to thicken the neck and, by extension, give a more masculine frame, with some also claiming jaw and facial changes. The exercise is popular on forums; there are no trials on appearance outcomes.

summary: Loaded forward neck flexion with a plate to thicken the neck; popular on forums, no appearance trials.
note: Forum users report soreness and, in one case, dizziness; no clinical data for this use.
currentQuick:
Neck curls with a plate are a weighted forward bend of the neck meant to build the muscles at the front and sides of the neck.
Forums post progress photos and debate whether the exercise affects the jaw or face. No studies have tested it for appearance.
How it works: Resistance on neck flexion works the sternocleidomastoid, which bends the neck forward when both sides contract.
Risks and caveats: Forum members report multi-day soreness and one reported dizziness and nausea. No clinical safety data on loaded neck curls for appearance are available.
deepLead:
Neck curls with a plate are a form of loaded neck flexion: a person lifts or holds a weight plate on the head while bending the neck forward, aiming to thicken the muscles at the front and sides of the neck. In looksmaxxing forums the exercise is discussed as a way to build a thicker neck and, by extension, a more masculine overall look.
Material on the exercise is limited to forum discussion, which this article cites only for what members say. No clinical trial of loaded neck curls for appearance is available among the sources used here. The muscle chiefly responsible for forward neck flexion, the sternocleidomastoid, is described in general anatomy references .

name: Shrugs / trap training

angle.text: Users train shrugs to build the upper trapezius, which fills the base of the neck and makes it look thicker. Sources reviewed cover muscle activation during the exercise, not its effect on how the neck looks.

summary: Loaded shoulder raises to build the traps and make the neck look thicker; sources cover only muscle activation, not looks.
note: Sources are thin; no appearance studies.
currentQuick:
Shrugs raise the shoulders against weight to train the upper trapezius. In looksmaxxing talk the muscle is linked to a thicker-looking neck.
Research exists on muscle activation during shoulder and neck exercises, but none on appearance.
How it works: Resistance on shoulder elevation works the upper trapezius; electromyography studies measure this activation in specific populations.
Risks and caveats: No harms are documented in the available sources. Height-gain claims from shrugs have not been studied.
deepLead:
Shrugs and trapezius training are resistance exercises in which the shoulders are raised against a load, used to build the upper trapezius muscle. In looksmaxxing discussion they are mentioned as a way to make the neck look thicker by building the muscles at its base.
Available research on shrug-type exercises concerns muscle activation and neck-pain rehabilitation rather than appearance. An electromyography study in women with chronic neck muscle pain measured activation of neck and shoulder muscles during selected strengthening exercises , and another evaluated muscle activity during a standardized shoulder resistance training bout in novices .
